ruling: The incident splits enforcement asymmetrically by legibility rather than by fault: the disclosed/frozen branch absorbs fast, cheap procedural tightening because regulators already have hooks into it, while the unfrozen/live branch — the one that actually produced the incident — escapes comparably costly action until new authority is built, widening the capability gap the segmentation stage already opened.
because: Every minute agrees the incident is a P6-delivered consequence that raises pressure, but they split sharply on where costly enforcement lands: ai-oversight-lag and pressure-model (round 2) both argue enforcement mechanically targets whichever branch is already legible to overseers, hitting the frozen branch first even though the unfrozen branch caused the harm, because building new audit/liability hooks takes a full oversight cycle. ai-pressure and ai-public-backlash instead assume attribution itself forces the executive or public sentiment to act directly on the offending (unfrozen) branch — but this requires a second assumption the brief never granted: that political will alone manufactures enforceable authority within the attribution window, rather than authority-building being the rate-limiting step. lab-moves and ai-regulation-teeth thread between these by keying off the named-defendant mechanism (a satisfied trigger-condition with an identifiable target bites regardless of branch), which is the most brief-faithful account since it doesn't require inventing new institutional capacity.
threat_live: the capability gap between the two branches widens rather than closes, because the branch that is easiest to regulate (frozen/disclosed) is the one that actually gets regulated, while the branch that caused the harm (unfrozen/concentrated) continues compressing its cycle time faster than any new oversight authority can be built to reach it
strongest_minute: ai-oversight-lag — it is the only minute that names the actual mechanism of asymmetry (oversight-cycle lag versus compressed cycle-time) rather than just asserting which branch 'wins' the incident's fallout, and it held that mechanism unchanged from round 1 to round 2 under direct challenge.
weakest_minute: ai-pressure — its round-1 claim that the executive resolves its stage-2 conflict by freezing the fast branch treats political resolution as automatic and instantaneous, and in round 2 it only restates the claim against pressure-model's objection without addressing why enforcement capacity would exist against a branch regulators cannot yet see into.
shared_assumption: All six minutes assume the incident is unambiguously and quickly attributed to a specific developer/branch, when the brief only grants 'clearly-attributable' as an incident property, not that attribution converts into actionable jurisdiction over an undisclosed branch within the same timeframe.
smuggled_assumption: ai-pressure smuggles in a second assumption beyond the brief: that the US federal executive uses this specific incident to resolve its unrelated stage-2 unilateral-preemption-vs-Senate-bill conflict in one direction, which imports an entire prior policy fork not established as settled by the incident alone.
unresolved: Whether the unfrozen branch's harm-producing developer faces ANY costly consequence at all within the window, versus only the frozen branch being touched — ai-regulation-teeth and pressure-model leave open whether the 120-day enforcement action lands on the named defendant regardless of which branch they're in, or whether 'named defendant' effectively only ever resolves to the legible (frozen) branch in practice.
